documents.abstract: Abstract While the ubiquitous adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) monitoring in construction projects has substantiated significant gains in operational efficiency and safety, its backlash remains theoretically underdeveloped. In practice, AI is gradually replacing human supervisors to monitor workers’ operation trajectories and work status. However, existing research has not yet unpacked workers’ cognition and behavioral responses toward AI monitoring. Therefore, grounded in the combination of psychological reactance theory and social exchange theory, the current study investigates how AI monitoring triggers counterproductive work behaviors and the boundary role of perceived organizational support. Through a survey of 352 on-site workers across diverse engineering projects, our findings reveal that AI monitoring is positively correlated with both production and political deviance. This relationship is mediated by negative cognition and anger, while perceived organizational support serves as a critical moderator that mitigates these detrimental effects. Furthermore, combined with the two supplementary studies, this research further verifies that the AI monitoring context triggers reactance among on-site workers when they perceive threats to freedom. By uncovering these distinct underlying mechanisms, this study extends the application of psychological reactance theory to the research context of AI monitoring on on-site workers in construction projects and develops a context-specific explanation.

Abstract The history of education, both in terms of teaching and of assessing students, is one of ever-increasing scope and breadth, with constant pressure on educators to do more, with more students, using as few resources as possible. For this reason, much of the practices associated with modern educational measurement (e.g., multiple-choice items) have been designed with efficiency in mind, rather than psychological validity. Today, generative artificial intelligence (AI) promises to yet-again increase the efficiency of education, by outsourcing some tasks typically done by human educators to AI. One area where AI has already been consistently applied is in the psychoeducational assessment of creative thinking, where AI appears to be able to score student responses to human-written tests, assemble assessment batteries of existing tasks, and even possibly write new assessments itself. In this chapter, we discuss the increase in efficiency that AI can bring to creativity assessment, while also considering how this increase in efficiency might exacerbate or even generate new validity issues, especially vis-à-vis the societal consequences of assessing the creativity of students from diverse cultural backgrounds and perspectives, using the same AI evaluator.

Background: Electronic prescribing (e-prescribing) and computerized provider order entry (CPOE) are increasingly used in medication management, but successful implementation depends on more than technology. How systems fit workflows, user practices, organizational conditions, and the policy environment can influence their use in routine care. Objective: To synthesize empirical evidence on barriers, facilitators, and other factors influencing e-prescribing/CPOE implementation in clinical practice. Methods: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed and Scopus were searched for empirical studies published from January 2000 through December 2025. Eligible studies directly examined barriers, facilitators, determinants, or implementation processes involving e-prescribing, CPOE, EPMA, or EMMS in clinical settings. Methodological quality was assessed at criterion level using MMAT 2018 without an overall numerical score. Results: The review included 49 reports representing 48 unique studies. Workflow disruption and workload were most frequent (46/48; 95.8%). Technical infrastructure/usability, perceived usefulness/safety/efficiency/time, acceptance/resistance/self-efficacy/trust, and leadership/organizational readiness/user engagement were each identified in 45/48 studies (93.8%). Training and implementation support occurred in 43/48 (89.6%), communication/interoperability/prescription processing in 38/48 (79.2%), and policy/financial/external-environment factors in 21/48 (43.8%). Conclusion: E-prescribing/CPOE implementation involves interconnected technical, workflow, human, organizational, and external factors. Workflow fit, organizational readiness, user involvement, implementation support, and policy and resource conditions require attention when systems are introduced or optimized. Theme frequencies indicate study-level presence rather than effect estimates.

This article reports on my action research study exploring the integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) into creative writing pedagogy at higher education level. Over twelve months, I conducted six pedagogical experiments across three London institutions, engaging fifty-two students in exploring AI’s functional dimensions: as ideation catalyst, collaborative tool, scaffolding mechanism, editorial assistant, research facilitator and assessment instrument. Using a critical realist framework, I examine what emerged from this systematic investigation: GenAI demonstrates clear affordances in particular contexts (research, translation, ideation generation) but significant limitations in others (editorial feedback, assessment, true creative collaboration). Students across all cohorts showed sophisticated critical awareness of AI’s training processes and ethical implications, and most remained cautious about deploying AI as a creative tool. The article argues that engaging with GenAI’s weaknesses might be its greatest pedagogical strength.

The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence in education raises a question that goes beyond efficiency: can AI support inclusive design without weakening teacher agency? This study examines that tension through Universal Design for Learning (UDL), understood not as a checklist of accommodations but as a framework for anticipating learner variability and removing barriers from the outset. The recent UDL 3.0 Guidelines further emphasise affect, identity, belonging and participation, making inclusive design inseparable from the relational dimension of teaching (CAST, 2024). The study introduces the construct of Digital Affective Literacy, defined as the capacity to preserve inclusive and relational intentionality while working with generative systems. This competence involves recognising the persuasive fluency of AI outputs, resisting uncritical delegation and transforming technological support into an opportunity for reflection. The construct is grounded in the relationship between emotion and cognition (Immordino-Yang & Damasio, 2007), in the risk of cognitive offloading (Risko & Gilbert, 2016), and in the Vygotskian distinction between tools that execute a task and mediators that reorganise thought (Vygotsky, 1978). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 49-50. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Social Robotics and Socio-Emotional Inclusion.

This study explores the attitudes of a sample of approximately 1,000 prospective support teachers towards Artificial Intelligence (AI) using the GAAIS scale. Although participants accept AI as an operational scaffolding tool, they strongly reject algorithmic delegation in professional decisions. Statistical uncertainty about didactic personalization highlights a profound awareness: true inclusion requires human relational care. The contemporary educational horizon is strongly impacted by advanced algorithmic systems, moving towards what Floridi (2025) defines as the onlife condition: an integrated ecosystem in which the boundaries between physical and digital dissolve. Within this framework, teachers face a dual pressure: on the one hand, the technocratic push towards automation, on the other the "Frankenstein complex", understood as an ancestral fear of a technological dehumanization and a marginalization of their role (Lim & Kim, 2024). This tension is particularly evident in special teaching, which is strongly focused on empathy. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 327-328. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI integration places teacher education at a critical crossroads for support teachers, whose identity is grounded in an ethics of care (Booth & Ainscow, 2008; d'Alonzo, 2017). The AIL framework requires holding the tension between innovation and relational pedagogy (Adamoli et al., 2026), as opposed to uncritical adoption (Chan & Lee, 2023; Williamson, 2024) or the Frankenstein Complex: resistance rooted in fear that AI impoverishes teaching's relational core (Selwyn, 2019). No prior study has jointly examined inclusive attitudes and AI co-agency in TFA Sostegno trainees. The general objective was to examine whether inclusive orientation predicts professional AI coagency. (RO1) Profile both constructs through cluster analysis; (RO2) test their relationship controlling for demographics; (RO3) test Deprivation as mediator of Concerns–Affordance via bootstrap (Preacher & Hayes, 2008). H1: Attitudes + Capability/Affordance (Ertmer, 2005). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 358-360. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.

The essay is part of the growing body of research on artificial intelligence in educational setting, focusing on the transformation of the emotional and relational aspect of generative and conversational system. Starting from the research question regarding how the recent educational literature conceptualizes, discusses and problematizes the emotional support mediated by artificial intelligence and its relationship between embodied care and human educational relationships, the study adopts a comparative review approach to analyse the different ways in which these dimensions are defined, articulated, and problematized. The analysis examines scientific publications released between 2022 and 2026, a timeframe that corresponds to the most intense period of dissemination and accessibility of artificial intelligence systems, capable of simulating dialogical interaction, emotional support, affective personalization in the educational context. Through a strict and transparent selection process conducted on major international databases, in particular Scopus, Web of Science and PsycINFO, the study constructs a heterogeneous corpus of empirical studies, theoretical contributions and reviews that share a focus on the socio-emotional dimension of education mediated by artificial intelligence. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 26-27. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Ontology of Care and the Simulation of Empathy.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reconfiguring educational systems, reshaping the tenets of knowledge and the relational dynamics of instructional practice. Within this transition, computational AI's evolution reconfigures educational systems, altering classroom ecology, dismantling vertical knowledge transmission, and shifting assessment toward higher-order skills (Luckin, 2018; Selwyn, 2019). Adopting a Critical AI Literacy framework (Veldhuis et al., 2025), this study emphasizes understanding algorithmic agency, ethical impacts, and algorithmic justice. Critical oversight operations rest on the Human-in-Command principle (Floridi, 2022), asserting assessment as a human prerogative rooted in a student's biography. This fosters an "augmented intelligence" where routine-free time enhances educational relationships, mitigating cognitive passivity from chatbots (Andler, 2024). Ultimately, Digital Affective Literacy empowers teachers as pedagogical directors of care (Pellerey, 2024). The study adopted a convergent parallel mixed methods design to analyse teachers' perceptions and self-efficacy levels regarding AI. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 315-316. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter identifies six aspects of creativity that reflect intrinsically human capacities and examines the human affordances that make them difficult for generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to authentically replicate. Although GenAI may appear to demonstrate these traits, it often reflects a sense of mimicry rather than genuine experience or intention. By drawing these distinctions, the chapter points to the limits of GenAI while also showing how it can support collaborative creative work and how human creativity can be extended rather than replaced by technological tools. The chapter closes with educational implications, arguing that cultivating these human aspects of creativity can help students approach human–GenAI collaboration with discernment, adaptability, and ethical awareness. The aim is not simply to ask whether GenAI can be creative but to help educators and researchers recognize and sustain moments in which human creative agency comes through in generative partnerships.

The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence in educational contexts has transformed how students encounter academic content, yet a fundamental question remains underexamined: Do English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners possess the critical literacy competencies needed to evaluate AI-generated texts? This study investigated whether students in Morocco’s Classes Préparatoires aux Grandes Écoles (CPGE)—one of the nation’s most academically selective post-secondary programs—demonstrate readiness for AI-era literacy demands. We developed a diagnostic assessment instrument, the Critical Reading Diagnostic Assessment (CRDA), designed to mirror common characteristics of AI-generated academic content: a confident, authoritative tone, a logical structure with subtle gaps, claims requiring verification, and culturally embedded assumptions. Thirty first-year CPGE students (M age = 18.6 years) evaluated argumentative passages across five critical dimensions: argument identification, evidence evaluation, assumption recognition, multi-source synthesis, and source criticism. Metacognitive self-assessment data were also collected. Results revealed systematic evaluation failures across all dimensions, with mean accuracy rates of only 18–39% and large effect sizes confirming substantial deficits (d = 1.11–2.25). Metacognitive analysis showed that students overestimated their abilities by 11–38 percentage points across all dimensions, indicating profound self-assessment inaccuracies.

Abstract In many corporate business organizations today, message misrouting has become a persistent problem among professional team members, because communications frequently reach unintended recipients and will therefore require manual redirection, this leads to delays in response times and disruption to workflow. There are existing message automation tools designed to handle this like Gmail filters, Slack workflows, Zapier, and Make but they rely largely on keyword or condition matching, which can perform poorly given the natural variability of message phrasing in real communication. This study presents the design and implementation of an intelligent message routing and triage platform that applies natural language classification to automatically process and route incoming Gmail and Slack messages. The platform integrates the LLaMA 3.1 large language model, which was accessed via the Groq API, with the Gmail and Slack APIs, enabling semantic rather than keyword-based classification. The design of the system allows users to define routing rules in plain English through a web-based dashboard, while a background polling service monitors connected inboxes every five minutes for new messages. Each incoming message is classified according to semantic intent against user-defined rules, triggering one of three actions (forwarding, automated reply, or ignoring) or, where no rule matches or the classifier flags the message for user action, escalation to a human reviewer, with every event logged for auditability. The system was developed iteratively across four development cycles and implemented as a full-stack TypeScript application using Next.js, Express.js, and MongoDB. The evaluation comprised functional testing, integration testing, and a preliminary feasibility check of the classifier. Functional testing achieved a 100% pass rate across all component categories (34 tests). The feasibility check used 14 author-constructed messages covering four of the six supported rule categories: 12 were matched to the intended rule (85.7%; 95% Wilson confidence interval 60.1–96.0%) and two were not matched and were escalated to human review, whereas a simulated keyword-matching baseline matched 5 of 14 (35.7%; 16.3–61.2%). Because the set is small, was written to avoid the rule wording, and was labelled by the authors, these figures illustrate the system's behaviour and do not establish comparative accuracy. Both unmatched messages involved indirect scheduling language not explicitly captured by rule conditions, indicating that classification performance remains sensitive to rule specificity. The key contribution is a documented system design, including an abstain-and-escalate decision rule, for embedding large language model classification into multi-channel business productivity tools, with particular relevance for Nigerian and African small and medium-sized enterprises seeking affordable, accessible, and intelligent communication automation.

documents.abstract: Generative AI tools have moved rapidly into professional and organizational practice, outpacing individuals' capacity to use them well. Fluent, superficially convincing outputs foster automation bias, the tendency to over-rely on automated systems and miss the errors they introduce (Goddard et al., 2012); field-experimental evidence shows AI assistance boosts performance within its current capability while just as reliably degrading it outside that boundary, a limit users cannot detect from fluency alone (Dell'Acqua et al., 2023; Fernandes et al., 2026). This motivates closer scrutiny of how AI literacy is measured. Most existing instruments rely entirely on self-report, including for the cognitive dimension (Ng et al., 2024), and show weak correlations with independently developed objective performance tests (Koch et al., 2024), with self-assessment errors that are not uniformly directional (Zhang et al., 2026). Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 158-159. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Hybrid and "Emotionally Aware" Learning Environments.

documents.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence into educational ecosystems does not merely constitute an instrumental addition; rather, it portends an ontological transformation that reconfigures contemporary regimes of truth, epistemic validation criteria, and processes of subjectification (Paparella, Mancarella, 2025). The core issue extends beyond evaluating whether algorithmic tools are beneficial or detrimental; instead, it demands an understanding of the structural conditions under which education can still authentically occur when the production of knowledge is structurally outsourced to predictive and automated systems. Within this conceptual landscape, the paradigm of the algorithmic self comes to the fore: an inflection of personal identity that is continuously co-constituted and reconfigured within a perpetual relational dialogue with digital technologies. Governed by the underlying logics of recommendation, profiling, and automated personalization, the algorithmic self is exposed to a progressive semantic impoverishment. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 21-22. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Ontology of Care and the Simulation of Empathy.

OBJECTIVES: To determine whether integrating an artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support system (VivoAID) into optical coherence tomography (OCT) interpretation improves diagnostic accuracy and efficiency for novice users evaluating basal cell carcinomas (BCCs). METHODS: Two dermatology research fellows completed a structured OCT training module for BCC identification using the VivoSight Dx system. Each independently reviewed 45 de-identified OCT scans (31 BCC-positive and 14 BCC-negative, negative ones included squamous cell carcinomas, keratoacanthomas, actinic keratoses and scar tissue), with ground truth established by expert clinical interpretation and histopathology, in two sessions: one unassisted and one AI-assisted. Session order was counterbalanced between learners, and scans were re-randomized for AI sessions. In unassisted sessions, learners manually classified scans; in AI-assisted sessions, they reviewed AI-annotated scans, recorded agreement/disagreement, and noted additional findings. Time-to-decision per scan was measured. A linear mixed-effects model in SAS assessed the effect of AI on decision time while accounting for scan difficulty. RESULTS: Without AI, correct BCC identification was 62% for Learner 1% and 64% for Learner 2 (combined 63%). With AI assistance, accuracy increased to 78% and 76%, respectively (combined 77%), reflecting relative improvements of 25% and 17% (combined +21%). Mean decision time decreased from 45 to 28 s for Learner 1 and from 35 to 22 s for Learner 2, yielding a combined reduction from 40 to 25 s (~38% faster). AI use significantly reduced decision time by an average of 15.1 s per image (p < 0.0001). AI standalone accuracy versus expert opinion was 64%, comparable to novice baseline performance. CONCLUSIONS: AI-enhanced OCT with VivoAID significantly improved novice users' diagnostic accuracy and efficiency, despite AI performance alone being similar to baseline novice interpretation. These data support VivoAID's role as a decision-support and potential educational tool in dermatology. Findings are limited by small sample size, single-institution design, and repeated review of the same scans. TRIAL REGISTRATION: None.

The growth and integration of cloud computing with other advanced technologies (such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and other security technologies and architectures) have introduced different cybersecurity challenges and opportunities that require academic investigation. This research conducts a bibliometric analysis of 1,583 papers from Scopus database between 2010 to 2026 trying to address four main research aims: (1) publication growth and productivity, (2) active contributors in the field, (3) themes and evolution of cloud security, and (4) emerging and research directions. The findings reveal an exponential growth, with annual output rising from 3 papers in 2010 to 358 in 2025, highlighting an annual growth rate exceeding 30%. Keyword analysis also reveals technical security evolutions: from cloud architecture and basic security (2010–2015), through threat, privacy, risk and intelligent detection (2016–2020), to current state dominated AI-driven approaches and other cutting edge technologies such as blockchain, edge computing, quantum cryptography and decentralized security (2021–2026). The results also show increased security complexity due to the integration of advanced technologies and secure architectures with the cloud such as decentralized security (e.g. federated learning also known as distributed AI models), AI driven cybersecurity, zero-trust architectures, privacy-preserving computation and advanced cryptography such as post-quantum cryptography. These technologies are among the most challenging emerging research areas, yet they are the most promising regarding cloud computing. Finally, as cybersecurity technologies evolve, security complexity of the cloud will continue to grow.

The rapid expansion of live-streaming commerce has transformed digital marketing by combining real-time product presentation, social interaction, entertainment, and purchasing functions on a single platform. Yet the literature remains dispersed across marketing, electronic commerce, information systems, and consumer behavior. This study maps the growth, intellectual foundation, thematic structure, and emerging directions of live-streaming marketing research. The population comprised English-language Scopus articles published from 2019 to 21 July 2026 that matched the title-abstract-keyword search logic for live streaming and marketing. Total sampling retained all 252 query-matched records after a duplicate audit found no repeated titles, DOIs, or EIDs. Descriptive performance analysis was combined with citation analysis and all-keyword co-occurrence, network, and overlay visualization using VOSviewer. Full counting and a minimum threshold of five occurrences produced 43 eligible keywords, of which 40 formed the largest connected network and five clusters. The findings show rapid growth after 2023 and themes concerning consumer psychology and impulse buying; social media, retailing, and strategy; technology, trust, and purchase intention; sales and influencer marketing; and the integration of live-streaming commerce into digital marketing. Artificial intelligence, virtual streamers, profitability, trust, and sales performance are the newest topics. The study offers an updated, marketing-specific map and supports more credible, transparent, technology-enabled, and performance-oriented live-streaming strategies.

The rapid adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) decision systems has increased organizational dependence on large-scale data, making big data governance a critical requirement for ensuring reliable and responsible decision-making. Although AI systems are often evaluated based on predictive accuracy and computational performance, their trustworthiness is strongly influenced by the quality, security, privacy, traceability, and fairness of the data used throughout the AI lifecycle. This study aims to develop a Big Data Governance Framework for Trustworthy AI Decision Systems by integrating key governance dimensions with trustworthy AI requirements. A qualitative conceptual framework development approach was employed, supported by structured literature review, thematic synthesis, and design science research principles. Relevant literature on big data governance, trustworthy AI, data quality, privacy, security, explainability, accountability, fairness, and AI decision systems was reviewed to identify recurring concepts and research gaps. The results show that trustworthy AI decision systems require seven core governance dimensions: data quality governance, security and privacy governance, metadata and data lineage, bias and fairness control, explainability support, accountability mechanisms, and continuous monitoring. These dimensions strengthen trustworthy AI capabilities, including reliability, transparency, explainability, fairness, privacy preservation, security, robustness, and auditability. The proposed framework demonstrates that trustworthy AI is not only determined by algorithmic performance but also by strong data governance across the AI lifecycle. This study concludes that effective big data governance can improve decision accuracy, traceability, accountability, risk reduction, and stakeholder trust in AI-based decision systems.

documents.abstract: Over the past decades, medical engineering has become embedded in nearly every aspect of modern healthcare. From the intensive care unit to the operating room and the rehabilitation clinic, patients are increasingly diagnosed, treated and, at times, kept alive by engineered devices and procedures. As outlined at the journal's inception in its original Field Grand Challenge (Pioletti, 2023), the field has grown at a remarkable pace, and nearly every major medical innovation now relies, directly or indirectly, on translating engineering concepts. Yet the value of such progress is ultimately measured where patients are treated: at the bedside, in the operating room and along the (often long) road to recovery.Here, we introduce a new section of Frontiers in Medical Engineering focused on biomedical engineering research towards clinical endpoints, namely research in which engineering principles, methods and devices are brought to patients within clinical care, and whose success is ultimately judged by outcomes in the patient (e.g. survival, complication rates or recovery of function). In what follows, we focus on three identified areas where engineering is most directly woven into clinical care: (i) organ support at the bedside, (ii) rehabilitation and assistive technologies, and (iii) surgical and interventional engineering. For each, we briefly outline where the field stands and what we see as some of the outstanding challenges. We then share some thoughts on small clinical pilot studies, where an engineering contribution meets patients for the first time, as one path of particular interest. Our hope is that the section will become a home for work that brings engineers and clinicians to the same table, with the patient as the common endpoint.Few places in the hospital rely as heavily on engineering as the intensive care unit. Mechanical ventilation, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) and temporary mechanical circulatory support all substitute, at least in part, for the function of failing organs. The COVID-19 pandemic served as a stark reminder of how central these technologies have become. At its peak, mechanical ventilation was arguably the most widely used form of acute organ support across the globe, and the experience gathered has since informed updated guidelines on respiratory support in acute respiratory distress syndrome (Grasselli et al., 2023). Research activity on ECMO has grown steadily in recent years, and the use of venovenous ECMO for severe respiratory failure is now supported by international guidelines (Tonna et al., 2021). In parallel, pooled data from randomized trials now inform the use of temporary mechanical circulatory support in cardiogenic shock (Thiele et al., 2024).Yet organ support remains, by design, a double-edged sword. Mechanical ventilation keeps patients alive while it can also injure the very lungs it is meant to protect (von Düring et al., 2025).Likewise, extracorporeal circuits expose blood to large foreign surfaces and non-physiological flows, such that thrombosis and bleeding remain among the most frequent complications (Chandler, 2022). In brief, these limitations are intimately tied to engineering: how mechanical loads, flows and interfaces translate into tissue damage in the patient. Such constraints are not readily captured by device settings or dose-based arguments alone. Rather, they call for experimental and clinical studies that link support strategies to biological markers of injury in the patient.A number of outstanding engineering challenges still lie ahead. First, there remains a need to move from device settings to patient outcomes and to understand which mechanical quantities (e.g. strain, flow or shear) predict injury in a given patient. Second, extracorporeal and circulatory support devices must become safer and simpler to deploy, so that they can be used beyond a handful of expert centres. Third, as automation enters the bedside (e.g. closed-loop control of ventilation or anaesthesia), such systems must be evaluated against clinical endpoints rather than technical performance alone; a recent multicentre trial, for example, found no gain in ventilatorfree days with automated closed-loop ventilation compared with protocolized conventional ventilation (Sinnige et al., 2026). Across these three challenges, these are research questions in their own right, calling for measurements and models that are tested early in patients together with clinical researchers.Stroke, spinal cord injury, limb loss as well as musculoskeletal conditions and injuries affect hundreds of millions of patients worldwide, with musculoskeletal disorders alone accounting for the largest share of the global need for rehabilitation (Cieza et al., 2020). For many of these patients, recovery of function, rather than survival, is the clinical endpoint that matters most.Beyond neurological rehabilitation, assistive biomechanical devices (e.g. orthoses, braces or soft wearable exosuits) are increasingly designed to support joints and muscles after injury or in chronic musculoskeletal conditions. Wearable exoskeletons, in particular, have drawn growing research interest in recent years, and rely on increasingly sophisticated designs and control strategies to assist walking (Siviy et al., 2023). At the same time, brain-computer interfaces are being explored to restore upper limb function after stroke (Li et al., 2025), and a Cochrane review of electromechanical-assisted gait training now provides pooled clinical evidence on its benefit (Mehrholz et al., 2020). In parallel, bionic limbs and neuroprosthetics have advanced from laboratory demonstrations towards clinical use, with neural interfaces that restore sensation and more intuitive control of prosthetic limbs (Huang et al., 2024).and what patients experience in daily life. We are well aware that engineering advances alone do not resolve this gap, which also depends on patient selection, therapy dosing and reimbursement, to cite a few. Nevertheless, we see some of the following challenges as central: (i) moving from short-term, laboratory based assessments to first studies in patients, with functional endpoints that matter to them; (ii) adapting devices to the variability between patients, and to the changes in a given patient over the course of recovery (Siviy et al., 2023); and (iii) bringing these technologies into the clinic and the home, where cost, usability and long-term adherence ultimately determine their impact, e.g. rates of upper-limb prosthesis rejection have changed little despite recent technological innovations (Salminger et al., 2022).The operating room has undergone a profound transformation over the past two decades. Robotassisted minimally invasive surgery is now routine in many specialties, and the research community has accumulated a decade of experience on how robots may assist, and increasingly act alongside, the surgeon (Dupont et al., 2021). All the meanwhile, the question has shifted from whether robots can perform surgical tasks to how much autonomy they should be given, and under which conditions. The first surgical robots with some level of autonomy have already been cleared by regulators, yet most remain at the lowest levels of autonomy (Lee et al., 2024). Equally, while artificial intelligence and haptic feedback promise to improve precision and safety, evidence of their benefit for patients remains limited.In parallel, cardiovascular interventions have moved steadily away from open surgery and towards catheter-based procedures. Here, engineering contributes on two fronts. On one hand, robotic and magnetically steered catheters are opening access to vessels that remain out of reach for manual navigation, and artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in their navigation (Yao et al., 2026). On the other hand, transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has become a standard of care for a growing population of patients, and patient-specific computational models of valve deployment are increasingly explored to anticipate complications such as paravalvular leakage before the procedure (Rauseo et al., 2026). Both lines of work bring engineering directly into the catheterization laboratory.Beyond the device itself, the learning curve of operators, the cost of such systems and uneven access across hospitals and countries all shape whether patients ultimately benefit. Concurrently, robotic platforms record large amounts of procedural data (e.g. instrument trajectories, forces or images), which could serve as objective measures of quality, provided they are linked to patient outcomes. A major challenge remains moving from feasibility to clinical benefit. This entails (i) defining how levels of autonomy should be validated, regulated and accepted by clinicians and patients; (ii) demonstrating that robotic and image-guided procedures, for example, improve clinical outcomes, and not only procedural metrics; and (iii) validating patient-specific planning tools for structural heart interventions against outcomes across patient populations, rather than one patient at a time.Across the three challenges outlined above, a common thread emerges. Whether the engineering contribution concerns a device, a procedure, a control strategy or a planning tool, it is ultimately judged in patients, by clinical endpoints rather than by technical performance alone. Clinical evaluation, regulatory science, usability and human factors, as well as the equity and sustainability concerns raised by Pioletti (2023), are therefore integral parts of each topic rather than standalone themes. This raises the question of how such contributions can best reach patients in the first place.Large randomized controlled trials remain the gold standard of clinical evidence, and rightly so.Yet they are costly, take many years and come late in the life of a medical technology, long after the key engineering choices have been made. All the meanwhile, the step that matters most to engineers, that is, the first use of a device or procedure in patients, remains comparatively underreported, being often regarded as too clinical for engineering journals and too preliminary for clinical ones.We argue that this gap deserves more attention. Among the many contributions the section welcomes, we see small clinical pilot studies as a path of particular interest, namely first-in-human, feasibility and early-phase studies in which an engineering contribution is tested in patients for the first time. Such studies may include a handful of volunteers and/or patients, and their aim is not to establish efficacy. Instead, they ask whether a technology can be used safely, whether it behaves in patients as it did in the laboratory, and which endpoints and patient groups a subsequent trial should target.To illustrate, a pilot study at the bedside may test whether a new support strategy changes the load on the organ as intended, as recently shown in twelve patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome, in whom ventilator settings guided by electrical impedance tomography reduced the mechanical power delivered to the lungs (Jimenez et al., 2023). In rehabilitation, a first-in-human study may follow a single patient over many months, both in the clinic and at home, as shown for a brain-spine interface that restored natural walking after spinal cord injury (Lorach et al., 2023).In the catheterization laboratory, a first-in-human study may test whether a robotic system can safely assist a structural heart intervention, as recently reported for robotic-assisted transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (Zhu et al., 2025). In each case, the study is small, but the questions it answers are precisely those that determine whether a larger trial is worth pursuing.In this spirit, the section would particularly welcome (i) first-in-human and feasibility studies of novel technologies, devices and procedures; (ii) pilot studies linking engineering parameters (e.g. device settings, control strategies or procedural planning) to early clinical endpoints; and (iii) reports that link laboratory and clinical data obtained with the same technology, following established reporting guidelines for pilot and feasibility studies.The benefit of biomedical engineering for patients will be decided, to a large extent, where research and engineering meet the patient: in the intensive care unit, throughout rehabilitation, and in the operating room and catheterization laboratory. In each case, the technology has matured to a point where the main question is no longer whether it works, but whether, for whom and under which conditions it improves clinical outcomes. Answering such questions calls for the full spectrum of research, from experimental and computational studies with a clear path to the patient, to first-inhuman and pilot studies, larger clinical evaluations, as well as reviews and perspectives.Ultimately, it requires engineering and clinical research to advance hand in hand, and it is precisely this convergence that the section aims to foster, with the patient as the common endpoint.

documents.abstract: Bodily self-consciousness (BSC) is based on the brain's integration of multisensory signals, visual, somatosensory and vestibular. Postural control represents the main interface between the body and BSC, regulating the dynamic body schema. Recent evidence demonstrates a bidirectional link between postural stability and emotional states, highlighting how anxiety negatively affects proprioception. At the same time, a sedentary lifestyle and chronic psychological stress stimulate neuroendocrine pathways in children that increase inflammatory markers, reduce mucosal immune defences. Traditional postural programmes are limited to two-dimensional feedback or mirrors, however, Artificial Intelligence applied to education (AIED) now enables 3D biological modelling and interactive multisensory feedback. This study evaluates the effectiveness of an innovative AI-guided postural programme in a multisensory environment (IPT-ME) compared with traditional postural treatment (TPT), analysing the combined impact on postural parameters, psycho-affective well-being and immunological profile. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 370-371. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Kinesiology and sport between education and performance in European area.

BREXAL: Integrating Application Monitoring, Maintenance Workflows and AI-Assisted Operational Analysis BREXAL is an AI-assisted application operations and monitoring platform designed to integrate application health monitoring, incident management, maintenance workflows, infrastructure monitoring, and operational analysis into a unified workspace. This research paper presents the architecture, implementation, data flow, and operational capabilities of BREXAL. The platform combines a Next.js and React frontend with a Python-based FastAPI backend, SQLAlchemy data models, and AI-powered services. The proposed system incorporates several key capabilities, including: Application Monitoring: Website uptime checks, response-time monitoring, and incident detection. Infrastructure Monitoring: CPU, memory, and disk utilization tracking through a Python-based monitoring agent. Incident Management: Incident tracking, status transitions, and operational activity records. Bug and Maintenance Management: Defect tracking, maintenance scheduling, and team collaboration. AI-Assisted Analysis: Gemini-powered root-cause hypotheses, operational summaries, and troubleshooting recommendations. Health Scoring: A weighted application health score based on uptime, bug severity, and maintenance compliance. Trend-Based Risk Analysis: Analysis of historical monitoring and server metrics to identify potential operational risks. The paper examines how deterministic monitoring mechanisms and generative AI assistance can work together while maintaining transparency, traceability, and human supervision over operational decisions. It also discusses important engineering considerations, including security, prompt injection, data validation, monitoring reliability, AI grounding, and performance evaluation. The study is based on a source-code inspection of the BREXAL software artefact and proposes a structured evaluation framework for future validation. It does not claim experimentally verified prediction accuracy or production-level performance improvements. Research Area: Artificial Intelligence, AIOps, Software Reliability Engineering, DevOps, Application Monitoring, Generative AI, and Incident Management. Project: BREXALResearch Focus: Integrating Application Monitoring, Maintenance Workflows and AI-Assisted Operational Analysis.

Abstract Despite the increasing emphasis on creativity in education policy and curricula, there remains a persistent gap in translating creativity into empirical, assessable learning outcomes in the classroom. Existing creativity assessments are often constrained by subjectivity, limited scalability, and a lack of integration into real-world classroom practice. Generative artificial intelligence (AI), with its ability to process vast amounts of data, detect patterns in student work, and provide personalized feedback, offers a transformational opportunity to close this gap. However, the implementation of AI-driven creativity assessment remains underdeveloped, and several research areas must be addressed to realize its full potential. This chapter explores specific challenges in empirically assessing creativity in classrooms, identifies how AI can provide more accurate and scalable assessments, and outlines concrete examples of AI applications across various subjects.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is a qualitatively different technology that brings unique affordances and challenges, requiring a fundamental shift in how its role in human learning and creativity is understood. This shift involves moving beyond viewing GenAI literacy as merely another subject to be taught in schools and toward providing students with opportunities to responsibly exercise their creative agency by building custom solutions with GenAI. This chapter introduces the Build to Learn, Learn to Create (BL-LC) approach, which supports this kind of learning. The chapter shares insights and experiences from designing and participating in a university course structured around the BL-LC approach and concludes with implications for future research and educational practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is profoundly transforming how individuals communicate, learn, and build relationships. In education, its impact extends beyond technology, reshaping the construction of meaning and the experience of encounters with others. The pedagogical question, therefore, concerns not only what artificial intelligence is capable of doing but also what risks being redefined when relationships are interpreted according to the criteria of efficiency, immediacy, and functionality (Panciroli & Rivoltella, 2023). Accordingly, although generative systems are now capable of simulating forms of dialogue, listening, and apparently empathic support, it becomes essential to distinguish the simulation of relationships from genuine relational experience. The production of coherent and personalized responses does not, in fact, entail responsibility, reciprocity, vulnerability, or participation in a shared history. It is precisely this distinction that makes care an indispensable interpretative category for understanding the meaning of contemporary education. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 31-32. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Ontology of Care and the Simulation of Empathy.

This case study examined a “dormitory-class-college” information-driven framework to improve student management in higher education. Based on multicase analysis, it identified flaws in traditional models: fragmented information, delayed responses, and unclear accountability. The framework used information technology (IT) to redefine roles and communication across levels, establishing structured feedback for efficient information sharing and agile decisions. By clarifying responsibilities and integrating information flow, it enhanced situational awareness and coordination. Findings showed that well-designed, IT-enabled channels improved management precision and responsiveness. The case offers practical lessons and a replicable model for institutions seeking digital transformation in student affairs, highlighting benefits and organizational considerations for successful IT integration in academic settings.

Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly entering educational practice as a tool for producing texts, designing materials and supporting instructional decisions. Its presence, though, does not concern only technical efficiency. It also affects the way educational language is perceived, especially when a message appears empathic, reassuring and pedagogically appropriate. The question addressed in this study is not whether AI can write correct educational responses, but whether such responses are recognized as expressions of care when their authorship is uncertain or attributed to either a teacher or an artificial system. Care is understood here not as emotional tone alone, but as a pedagogical relation grounded in attention, responsibility and situated judgment (Noddings, 2005). The study adopts an exploratory mixed-methods design with a quantitatively driven structure and an integrated qualitative component. An anonymous online questionnaire was administered to 807 participants enrolled in teacher qualification pathways at Link Campus University. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 354-355. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. Volume DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23211262. Section: Teacher Education Between the "Frankenstein Complex" and the D-Generation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can streamline article screening and data extraction to accelerate meta‐analysis synthesis; however, their use remains limited in agrisciences. In this study, we evaluated the potential of LLMs to accurately extract data from articles of a published meta‐analysis. We developed a multi‐agent LLM (GPT and Gemini) pipeline that screened and extracted data from a set of 50 peer‐reviewed studies. When the LLMs disagreed, a structured human‐in‐the‐loop protocol was implemented to resolve the inconsistencies. Then, the pooled effect size estimates generated from the LLMs and human‑in‑the‑loop workflow were analyzed and compared to the meta‑analysis. Of 671 effect sizes reported in the published meta‐analysis, GPT recovered 180 effect sizes, and Gemini extracted 244 effect sizes, while the human‐in‐the‐loop recovered 293 effect sizes. Human reviewers had to verify 71.5% of all extracted effect sizes. The remaining 28.5% of the extracted effect size cases did not require manual review. These results demonstrate limited efficiency of GPT and Gemini to synthesize and extract data from articles regarding the effect of cover crop termination timing on soybean [ Glycine max (L.) Merr.] yield. Accurate data extraction remains dependent on literature reporting practices, highlighting the need for standardized, machine‐readable formats to support reliable AI‐assisted evidence synthesis in agricultural science.

Robotic living donor hepatectomy (R-LDH) aims to improve the safety and experience of healthy donors by combining three-dimensional visualization, wristed instrumentation, precision, and stable ergonomics with the benefits of minimal access. This review article summarizes current evidence and offers a pragmatic approach for centers to transition from open to routine robotic donation. Available evidence from retrospective feasibility series, matched cohorts, multicenter analyses, and registry data suggests that R-LDH may reduce donor morbidity compared to open and some evidence of fewer recipient biliary complications, although current evidence remains heterogeneous and largely non-randomized. Available comparative data, including single-center and international registry analyses, suggest lower morbidity with the robotic approach than with laparoscopy, although these comparisons remain limited and would benefit from confirmation in prospective multicenter studies. Learning-curve studies and prospective series suggest that with standardized technique, simulation, and early proctorship, proficiency appears achievable within a limited number of cases, with reduced complications over time. A center-readiness structure focused on “People” (trained team), “Process” (protocolized pathways with explicit conversion criteria), “Platform” (reliable robot access, ICG, ERAS), and “Proof” (prospective audit and external validation) supports phased adoption from standard to complex anatomy. Persistent barriers include limited robotic platform access, scheduling constraints, heterogeneity in reporting, and incomplete cost data, though shorter hospital stay, less pain, and faster return to normal daily activities may partially or potentially offset procedural costs in high-volume programs. In appropriately prepared centers, routine consideration of R-LDH for eligible donors may represent a reasonable donor-centered strategy. Concrete steps are outlined that surgeons and hospital leaders can undertake to implement R-LDH safely, monitor outcomes, and improve equitable access.

Cancer stem cells (CSCs) are a small population of cancer cells that endow unique traits of self-renewal, differentiation, tumorigenicity, quiescence and therapeutic resistance, ultimately leading to cancer relapse and poor prognosis. Conventional chemo- and radiotherapies effectively destroy rapidly dividing cancer cells; however, CSCs are largely refractory to these treatments due to special characteristics that include metabolic plasticity, low reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, apoptosis inhibition and modified DNA repair systems, effectively hijacking the tumour microenvironment and evading host immune surveillance. This review summarises the potential CSC diagnostic methods that can be used in routine clinical investigation for tailoring personalised treatment plans both pre- and post-surgery. In this way, a CSC gene signature, reactivity and load can be estimated and, by using artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms in a personalised therapeutic regimen, the most effective treatment response can be predicted. Furthermore, we propose incorporation of CSC-targeted therapies in conjugation with conventional chemo- and radiotherapies to eradicate CSCs, thereby eliminating the risk of relapse and therapy failure in cancer patients. This review also describes multiple potential molecular targets that may be used to target CSCs and emphasises the need for further evaluation, in order that they may be applied clinically.

Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education, yet its successful institutional adoption extends beyond technological capability to require effective knowledge governance, organizational readiness and coordinated decision-making. This study aims to structurally model the CSFs for GenAI adoption in education using an integrated interpretive structural modeling (ISM)–DEMATEL approach. The authors frame GenAI adoption explicitly as a knowledge management problem, analyzing how governance, infrastructure and privacy conditions enable or inhibit institutional capabilities for creating, sharing and governing GenAI-empowered knowledge. Design/methodology/approach The authors identified ten CSFs through a structured literature review and classified them as enablers, capabilities or outcomes across governance, infrastructure, data privacy, analytics, user experience and academic integrity. To analyze the causal and hierarchical relationships among CSFs, an expert validation was conducted through DEMATEL analysis by 20 experts, followed by ISM modeling, which involved 16 experts. Findings DEMATEL identifies technical infrastructure and scalability (CSF-V), data privacy and security (CSF-VII) and integration with LMS/SSO/enterprise systems (CSF-IX) as prominent causal factors. ISM further positions CSF-V at the deepest foundational level, followed by AI governance, policy and ethics (CSF-III), while assessment integrity and academic honesty (CSF-X) occupies the terminal dependent level. The findings identify assessment integrity (CSF-X), prompt literacy (CSF-IV) and user experience (CSF-VI) as dependent factors, confirming that they emerge from structural readiness rather than acting as independent adoption determinants. Research limitations/implications Results are restricted to expert judgment and defined CSFs, which can reduce generalizability across diverse educational settings. Future research must involve larger samples, validate empirically and use longitudinal designs to study changing relations while also testing the knowledge governance mechanisms revealed in this research. Practical implications The model enables phased prioritization of CSFs for optimal implementation of GenAI. Foundational readiness requires infrastructure, system integration and data governance, followed by governance policies and faculty capacity development, before addressing user experience and academic integrity as dependent outcomes. Originality/value The research provides a systems approach to GenAI adoption in education by presenting an integrated ISM–DEMATEL framework based on TOE and DOI, grounded in knowledge governance theory. It aids authors’ understanding of how technological, organizational and knowledge governance dimensions must be sequentially aligned to enable better implementation of GenAI.

Background: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into creative practice raises new questions for craft-based disciplines such as ceramic design, where digital ideation must ultimately be translated into physical, material form. Objectives: This study explores (RQ1) where and why the alignment of AI-generated concept imagery with hand-built ceramic outcomes fails; (RQ2) how prompt-based iteration with a general-purpose text-to-image model supports or hinders the progressive refinement of a single design; and (RQ3) what forms of human knowledge and intervention are necessary to translate AI-generated concepts into producible ceramic objects. Methods: Using a qualitative, practice-based methodology, the researcher employed a text-to-image generative AI tool (ChatGPT 4 Plus + DALL·E 3) to generate design concepts for three ceramic objects—a children’s plate, a house number plaque, and a wall panel—which were subsequently produced by hand in collaboration with a professional ceramic instructor. Results: In the hands of a designer with limited ceramic experience, production difficulties clustered where the AI image encoded constraints that were invisible to the prompt—contour line weight, color separation in small recesses, lettering, scale and modular tolerance. AI-generated alternatives were frequently visually compelling yet materially infeasible, and the tool could not support incremental refinement of a single design across prompts. Whether these failures reflect properties of the AI output or the maker’s skill ceiling cannot be fully separated in a single-operator study; what follows is therefore a provisional, criteria-stated attribution, in which each breakdown is assigned to its most plausible source and the residual uncertainty is flagged. Conclusion: Generative AI functioned as a co-creative ideation partner rather than an autonomous designer; the negotiation between AI-proposed imagery and material reality was carried out by the human maker, drawing on codified technical knowledge (firing, shrinkage, dimensions) as well as tacit, embodied skill (brushwork, contouring, judging what will “work in clay”).

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex reasoning tasks through multi-agent collaboration. However, existing approaches primarily focus on open-ended reasoning or simple task decomposition and lack structured frameworks for long-horizon decisionmaking with explicit planning, execution, and supervision. To address this, we propose Chain-of-Agents Planner (CoA-Planner), a framework that explicitly coordinates Planning Agents, Worker Agents, and a Supervisor Agent through a structured task graph. The Planning Agent decomposes complex tasks into a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks with dependencies,Worker Agents execute specialized subtasks, and the Supervisor Agent monitors progress and resolves conflicts at critical milestones. Our framework introduces adaptive role reconfiguration that dynamically adjusts agent assignments based on historical performance metrics. We evaluate CoA-Planner on several long-context benchmarks including document analysis (50K-120K tokens), codebase review, and technical report generation. Experimental results show that CoA-Planner achieves an average success rate of 67.9%, outperforming single-agent LLMs by 23.5 percentage points (pp), Chain-of-Thought with RAG by 17.9pp, and existing Chain-of-Agents frameworks by 10.4pp. The framework demonstrates efficient scaling with 4-5 worker agents and reduces error rates across all categories, particularly in context coverage and reasoning consistency.

ABSTRACT Background Generative artificial intelligence can facilitate task completion, but whether it improves learning or consistently shapes task‐related emotions remains unclear. Objectives This mixed‐methods classroom study compared literary translation with ChatGPT access, translation with dictionary access and optional teacher assistance and regular instruction, focusing on tense accuracy and task‐related emotional experiences. Methods The study involved 42 English‐major undergraduates. All participants completed a pretest and a posttest of English tense use. The 29 students in the translation conditions completed six translation tasks and provided 556 repeated emotion‐bar records with concurrent written explanations; 10 of these students also participated in interviews. Robust analysis of covariance, within‐participant models, exploratory configurational measures and thematic analysis were used. Results Mean scores increased in all three conditions, but adjusted posttest scores and gain scores did not differ significantly among them. No statistically significant between‐condition differences were detected in individual‐emotion percentages or configurational measures. None of the six emotion percentages varied significantly across task sessions, although curiosity was lower at the fourth than at the first measurement point. Profile mixedness was lower in Task 5 (Session 6) than in Task 2 (Session 3). Qualitative findings linked emotions mainly to text content and difficulty, progress, time pressure and classroom conditions. ChatGPT was valued for its speed and immediacy but raised concerns about reliability, effort and ownership. Conclusion The study did not detect a statistically significant advantage for ChatGPT support in tense accuracy or emotional experience. The exploratory configurational analysis nevertheless identified a task‐session difference not apparent in the separate emotion percentages, illustrating the value of examining learning outcomes, repeated emotion reports and students' appraisals together when evaluating AI‐supported language tasks.

ChatGPT has become a part of the second language (L2) writing process as learners brainstorm ideas, seek feedback, and revise their texts. However, its pedagogical value depends on whether these interactions sustain behavioural, cognitive, and affective student engagement or contribute to disengagement. This systematic review synthesises research on ChatGPT-assisted L2 writing in the context of higher education concerning student engagement, examining patterns in research methods, theoretical perspectives, thematic findings, and future directions. The findings indicate that ChatGPT may both support and constrain student engagement, depending on learner characteristics, task design, feedback quality, and teacher guidance. The included studies highlighted that behaviourally, learners participated in planning and revision, but some relied heavily on artificial intelligence (AI) generated suggestions. Cognitively, ChatGPT prompted feedback evaluation and reflection, while inaccurate responses and cognitive offloading could limit deeper engagement. Affectively, learners reported motivation and reduced writing anxiety alongside frustration and a lack of interpersonal support. To organise the factors associated with both engagement and disengagement, the review proposes the preliminary ChatGPT-Enabled Smart Learning Environment (CESLE) framework which integrates engagement and disengagement factors and advances the concept of Ethical Human–AI Synergy through algorithmic stewardship, ethical collaborative intelligence, and an AI + teacher approach. The framework offers a context-sensitive foundation for supporting learner agency, responsible AI use, and sustained engagement in ChatGPT-assisted L2 writing. Thus, the review underscores the need for teacher-guided integration of AI that supports learners’ critical judgement and authorial voice.

This qualitative study examines how Filipino university students integrate ChatGPT into their language-learning practices, with particular attention to translanguaging and multilingual meaningmaking. Data were collected through an open-ended questionnaire completed by 21 university students and follow-up semi-structured interviews with five of these participants. The data were analyzed thematically to examine how students use ChatGPT across English, Filipino, and regional languages, as well as the perceived affordances and limitations of GenAI-mediated language learning. The findings suggest that students engage ChatGPT as a mediational and collaborative resource, not just as a corrective tool. Participants described strategically drawing on their multilingual repertoires to support comprehension, writing, and engagement with academic content, reflecting a distributed form of language learning shaped by linguistic, affective, and technological resources. At the same time, participants reported issues in their use of ChatGPT, particularly when English-centered norms and generic AI-generated outputs marginalized or constrained minoritized languages. The study highlights ChatGPT’s potential to support multilingual meaning-making while also showing how GenAI can reproduce dominant language hierarchies. Implications for multilingual language education and GenAI-informed pedagogy are discussed.

Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by patients and clinicians to obtain health-related information, yet their reliability in neck pain and interventional pain management remains uncertain. This study compared ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro using a multidimensional, short-term repeated-assessment framework evaluating clinical performance, safety, readability, expert assessment, and temporal consistency. Methods A standardized, investigator-developed set of 50 neck pain-related questions included patient-oriented questions, interventional pain management, safety and red-flag scenarios, and clinical vignettes. The same questions were submitted to both models at Week 0 and Week 2, with one response obtained for each model–question–time-point combination. Responses were anonymized, and evaluators were blinded to model identity. Accuracy, completeness, usefulness, and guideline adherence were assessed using predefined 5-point ordinal Likert-type scales, while red-flag omission, hallucinated facts, and overconfident inappropriate recommendations were evaluated as binary outcomes. Readability was assessed for patient-oriented questions, and reviewer comment scores were independently assigned by two evaluators. Analyses were exploratory, with no formal adjustment for multiple comparisons; p-values < 0.05 were considered nominally statistically significant. Results Two hundred responses were evaluated. At Week 0, Gemini had higher completeness and usefulness scores, whereas no nominally significant between-model differences were observed for accuracy or guideline adherence. At Week 2, ChatGPT had higher completeness scores, whereas Gemini had higher guideline adherence and usefulness scores; no nominally significant difference was observed for accuracy. Reviewer comment scores were lower for Gemini at both time points. Several within-model between-time-point differences were nominally significant but were interpreted as short-term variation rather than evidence of true longitudinal change. No nominally significant between-model differences were observed in the interventional pain management subgroup. Red-flag omissions were more frequent with ChatGPT than Gemini at Week 0 (24% vs. 8%; p = 0.008), whereas no nominally significant between-model difference was observed at Week 2. No nominally significant between-model differences were observed for hallucinated facts or overconfident inappropriate recommendations. ChatGPT had higher Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level scores at both time points, indicating greater textual complexity. Inter-rater reliability for reviewer comment scores ranged from good to excellent. Conclusions ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3 Pro generally received high scores within the predefined evaluation framework, but between-model differences varied by outcome and assessment time point and did not consistently favor either model. Differences between Week 0 and Week 2 should be interpreted as short-term variation in observed model output rather than evidence of true improvement or deterioration. These findings support multidimensional, time-specific evaluation of LLMs. LLMs should be regarded as informational or decision-support tools rather than substitutes for professional clinical reasoning or individualized clinical decision-making, particularly in safety-critical or interventional contexts.

documents.abstract: Fibromyalgia manifests as chronic widespread pain combined with fatigue, sleep disturbance, cognitive impairment ("fibro fog"), various somatic complaints, and anxiety-depressive symptoms. Chronic nonspecific musculoskeletal pain (CNSMP) in the neck and back may present under the mask of fibromyalgia. The approaches to managing patients with fibromyalgia and CNSMP in the neck and back differ. In fibromyalgia, antidepressants and anticonvulsants are effective as pharmacological agents, whereas in CNSMP of the neck and back, non-steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are effective. We present the observation of a female patient who, before seeking care at the Clinic of Nervous Diseases (CND) of Sechenov University, had been followed up with a diagnosis of fibromyalgia and had not responded to the prescribed pharmacotherapy (an antidepressant). At the CND, the patient was diagnosed with CNSMP of several localizations (cervicobrachialgia, lumboischialgia with myofascial pain syndrome) and concomitant episodic migraine. The patient's treatment was carried out in accordance with the established diagnoses and included optimal pharmacotherapy with NSAIDs (stepwise therapy with Dexalgin and a short course of Dexalgin 25 for the treatment of CNSMP, eletriptan for the relief of migraine), kinesiotherapy, training in ergonomic principles, optimal physical activity and correct postures in daily life, and cognitive-behavioral therapy for pain. The comprehensive therapy allowed the patient to cope with the pain syndromes relatively quickly and for a long period.
topics: Fibromyalgia and Chronic Fatigue Syndrome Research

documents.abstract: Introduction: Adaptive polyarticulated myoelectric hands aim to improve grasp versatility and intuitiveness of use; however, objective clinical and biomechanical evidence supporting their functional impact remains limited. Case presentation: A 75-year-old right-hand-dominant male with a long-standing transradial traumatic amputation and over 30 years of experience with a myoelectric tridigital prosthesis underwent experimental evaluation of an adaptive polyarticulated myoelectric hand (Adam’s Hand®). Methods: Assessment included patient-reported outcome measures (Orthotics and Prosthetics User Survey—Upper Extremity Functional Status (OPUS-UEFS), Trinity Amputation and Prosthesis Experience Scales–Revised (TAPES-R), Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand questionnaire (DASH), Short Form Health Survey 36 (SF-36)), standardized performance-based functional tests (Minnesota Manual Dexterity Test (MMDT), Box and Block Test (BBT), Southampton Hand Assessment Procedure (SHAP)), and laboratory-based biomechanical evaluation using optoelectronic motion capture and surface electromyography during Pointing, Hand-to-Mouth, and Grasping tasks. The adaptive prosthesis was tested after rapid artificial intelligence-based calibration, without structured training. Results: Patient-reported outcomes reflected high satisfaction and adaptation to the habitual prosthesis. Performance-based tests favored the habitual device in speed and dexterity, whereas the adaptive hand enabled additional grasp patterns. Biomechanically, the adaptive hand was smoother and faster during reaching, but less stable during grasping. Compensatory trunk and shoulder movements occurred with both devices, with a trend toward less compensation during reaching with the adaptive hand. Conclusions: This case highlights a task-dependent biomechanical profile of an adaptive polyarticulated myoelectric hand under first-use conditions. Rapid calibration may support immediate use for reaching, while optimal grasp control appears to require structured training.

Non-dilated left ventricular cardiomyopathy (NDLVC) presents a unique clinical paradox: patients with nearly identical phenotypes can face radically different clinical outcomes. NDLVC has been recently recognized as a distinct dynamic phenotype within the spectrum of non-ischemic cardiomyopathies, linked by a high risk of life-threatening arrhythmias. Recent advances in genetics have overcome clinical phenotyping in prognostic accuracy. Specifically, gene-specific scores have been introduced to guide primary prevention ICD in high-risk gene carriers. On the other hand, while gene-elusive cases present a more favourable arrhythmic profile, their long-term clinical outcome is more challenging to predict. Despite advancements in therapeutic strategies, the heterogeneity of the disease represents an ongoing dilemma for risk stratification and long-term surveillance. This review offers a comprehensive analysis of NDLVC management in clinical practice, highlighting the profound prognostic divergence between genetic (both in actionable and VUS carriers) and gene-elusive cohorts. By synthesizing current evidence, we aim to clarify how genotype–phenotype correlations influence clinical outcomes and to provide a framework for more personalized approaches in the follow-up and treatment of these distinct patient populations. Furthermore, we address the current lack of standardized guidelines specifically tailored to gene-elusive phenotypes. In conclusion, NDLVC management requires a paradigm shift towards a multi-parametric, genotype-directed framework, where cardiac magnetic resonance tissue characterisation and personalized risk scores are essential to optimize sudden cardiac death prevention. Future research must leverage artificial intelligence and polygenic risk scores (PRSs) to integrate multi-parametric clinical-imaging data and refine risk stratification beyond traditional binary models. Concurrently, human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) will be pivotal as a translational platform to clarify VUS pathogenicity, unravel gene-specific arrhythmic mechanisms, and accelerate targeted therapeutic interventions.

Background : Adverse drug events (ADEs) account for nearly 50% of preventable medical harm globally and place a burden on health care systems. Conventional pharmacovigilance based on spontaneous reporting faces challenges such as underreporting, low data quality, and delays in detecting safety signals. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are increasingly being applied to address these limitations, but evidence of their effectiveness and barriers to implementation remain scattered. Objective : To analyze the progress, effectiveness, benefits, and challenges of applying AI in pharmacovigilance, including signal detection, ADE prediction, clinical information extraction, causality assessment, and regulatory integration. Methodology : This study employed a narrative review of articles on AI and ML in pharmacovigilance and drug toxicity prediction. The literature included systematic reviews, scoping reviews, predictive modeling studies, and WHO policy documents. Results: Statistical methods such as PRR, ROR, BCPNN, and MGPS are still used because they are simple and auditable, despite their limited sensitivity. ML models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, logistic regression, and transformers like BERT and GPT show promising performance in the detection and prediction of ADEs, with accuracies of up to 94%. However, external validation, class imbalance, and interpretability remain challenges. Conclusion : AI has the potential to improve the efficiency and accuracy of pharmacovigilance, but requires improved data quality, real-world validation, model transparency, methodological standardization, and ongoing integration into clinical workflows.
